Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR A 180 MB, 400 k‑polygon GeoJSON is far beyond what a browser can parse and render in a single request. The only reliable fix is **to stop feeding the whole file to MapLibre** and replace it with a tiled, simplified, and (if possible) server‑side source. Below is a step‑by‑step “road‑map” you can follow right now, plus a few quick‑win tricks you can try while you’re waiting for the tiles to be generated. --- ## 1. Why GeoJSON fails at this size | What happens | Why it matters | |--------------|----------------| | **Full download** – the whole 180 MB file is fetched before anything is drawn. | Mobile networks, throttling, or a slow connection will stall for seconds‑to‑minutes. | | **Full parse** – the browser must turn the text into a JavaScript object (`JSON.parse`). | Parsing 400 k polygons can take > 3 s on a desktop and > 10 s on a phone, often freezing the UI thread. | | **Full render** – every polygon becomes a WebGL buffer. | WebGL has limits on vertex count; 400 k polygons (often millions of vertices) can exhaust GPU memory and crash the tab. | | **No level‑of‑detail** – every feature is drawn at every zoom. | At low zoom you’re drawing far more geometry than needed, wasting bandwidth and GPU cycles. | The MapLibre spec itself calls out these limits in the **GeoJSON performance thresholds** table (see the skill). You’re well past the “Crash zone”. --- ## 2. Quick‑win “stop‑gap” tricks (still not a long‑term solution) | Trick | What it does | How to apply | |-------|--------------|--------------| | **Simplify & reduce precision** | Removes unnecessary vertices and rounds coordinates, often cutting size 2‑5×. | Use **mapshaper** (CLI or web UI): `mapshaper input.geojson -simplify 0.5 -precision 5 -o format=geojson output.geojson` | | **Chunk the file** | Split into several smaller GeoJSON files (e.g., one per tile or per region) and load only the ones that intersect the viewport. | `ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON -where "ST_Intersects(geom, ST_MakeEnvelope(...))" chunk_01.geojson source.gpkg` – then add each as a separate source with `maxzoom`/`minzoom` filters. | | **Client‑side tiling with geojson‑vt** | Turns a GeoJSON into vector tiles *in the browser* so MapLibre only draws what’s visible. | ```js\nimport geojsonvt from 'geojson-vt';\nconst tileIndex = geojsonvt(geojson, {maxZoom: 14, tolerance: 3});\nmap.addSource('my-tiles', {type: 'vector', tiles: [], getTile: (z,x,y)=>{…}});\n```
**Caveat:** you still have to download the whole file first, so this only helps with rendering, not with network load. | | **Web‑Worker parsing** | Off‑load `JSON.parse` to a worker so the UI thread doesn’t freeze. | ```js\nconst worker = new Worker('parse-geojson-worker.js');\nworker.postMessage(url);\nworker.onmessage = e => map.addSource('my-data', {type:'geojson', data:e.data});\n```
Again, you still hit memory limits for 400 k polygons. | | **Use a raster fallback** | If you only need a visual “background” of the polygons, pre‑render them to raster tiles (PNG/WebP) and use a `raster` source. | Generate raster tiles with GDAL (`gdal2tiles.py`) or MapTiler, then add: `{type:'raster', tiles:['https://…/{z}/{x}/{y}.png']}`. | > **Bottom line:** these tricks can buy you a few seconds of usability, but they won’t scale. The proper fix is to **serve the data as vector tiles** (or raster tiles if you don’t need interactivity). --- ## 3. The “right” solution: Convert to vector tiles ### 3.1 Choose a tile format | Format | When to pick it | Pros | Cons | |--------|----------------|------|------| | **PMTiles** (single‑file archive) | You want a *serverless* solution (static storage on S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, etc.) | No tile server to run, HTTP range requests fetch only needed bytes, easy to version. | Updating requires re‑uploading the whole file. | | **MBTiles** (SQLite) | You already have a tile server that reads MBTiles (e.g., Martin, TileServer‑GL). | Widely supported, easy to edit with `sqlite3`. | Requires a running tile server to serve the tiles. | | **XYZ / TileJSON** | You have an existing tile server that serves plain `{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` URLs. | Simple URL template, works with any server. | No built‑in metadata; you must maintain TileJSON yourself. | > **Recommendation for most projects:** generate a **PMTiles** archive and host it on a CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Cloudflare R2 + Workers, or GitHub Pages). This gives you the same performance as a hosted tile service without any server‑side code. ### 3.2 Generate the tiles #### 3.2.1 Prepare the source data 1. **Simplify & quantize** – do this *before* tiling, otherwise tippecanoe will have to simplify each tile individually (much slower). ```bash # Using mapshaper (CLI) mapshaper input.geojson \ -simplify 0.5 \ -precision 5 \ -proj wgs84 \ -o format=geojson simplified.geojson ``` 2. **Clip to the area you actually need** – if you only need a country or a city, extract that extent with `ogr2ogr` or `mapshaper`. This reduces tile count dramatically. #### 3.2.2 Tile with **tippecanoe** (the most battle‑tested tool) ```bash # Install tippecanoe (brew, apt, or from source) # Example command for polygons: tippecanoe \ --output=parcel.pmtiles \ --layer=parcels \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --simplify-only-low-zooms \ --no-feature-limit \ --no-tile-size-limit \ --force \ simplified.geojson ``` **Key flags explained** | Flag | Why you need it | |------|-----------------| | `--minimum-zoom` / `--maximum-zoom` | Limit the zoom range to what you actually display (e.g., 5‑14). | | `--drop-densest-as-needed` | Tippecanoe will automatically drop the most detailed features when a tile would exceed the 500 KB limit, keeping the map responsive. | | `--simplify-only-low-zooms` | Keeps high‑zoom detail while aggressively simplifying low‑zoom tiles. | | `--no-feature-limit` / `--no-tile-size-limit` | Prevent tippecanoe from silently discarding features; you’ll see warnings instead. | | `--force` | Overwrites an existing file. | **Result:** a `parcel.pmtiles` file that is typically **10–30 MB** (depends on simplification) and contains all zoom levels you asked for. #### 3.2.3 Verify the tile schema Tippecanoe writes a TileJSON block inside the PMTiles file. You can inspect it with the `pmtiles` CLI: ```bash pmtiles inspect parcel.pmtiles ``` Look for the `vector_layers` array – it will contain a single layer named `parcels` with its attribute fields. You’ll need that name when you reference the source in your style (`source-layer: "parcels"`). #### 3.2.4 Host the PMTiles file - **Static storage** (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel) – just upload the file and make it publicly readable. - **CORS** – ensure the bucket/CDN sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). Most CDNs add this automatically for public objects; otherwise add a bucket policy or edge‑function header. > **Tip:** If you use Cloudflare R2, enable **“Range Requests”** (default) – MapLibre will request only the byte ranges it needs. ### 3.3 Add the source to MapLibre ```javascript // 1️⃣ Add the PMTiles source (requires the pmtiles plugin) import { PMTiles } from 'pmtiles'; const pmtiles = new PMTiles('https://my-cdn.com/parcel.pmtiles'); map.addProtocol('pmtiles', pmtiles.protocol); // 2️⃣ Define the source map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', url: 'pmtiles://parcel.pmtiles' // note the custom protocol }); // 3️⃣ Add a layer (example: fill polygons) map.addLayer({ id: 'parcel-fill', type: 'fill', source: 'parcels', 'source-layer': 'parcels', // matches the layer name from TileJSON paint: { 'fill-color': '#0066ff', 'fill-opacity': 0.3 } }); ``` If you prefer a plain XYZ URL (e.g., you run a tile server), the source definition would be: ```json { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["https://my-server.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"], "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14 } ``` --- ## 4. Alternative: Use a hosted vector‑tile service If you don’t want to manage the tile generation pipeline yourself, you can upload the GeoJSON to a hosted provider that will do the tiling for you: | Provider | Free tier / pricing | How to upload | |----------|--------------------|---------------| | **MapTiler Cloud** | 100 k features free, then $5/GB/month | Upload GeoJSON → “Custom Tileset” → auto‑generates PMTiles + TileJSON. | | **Protomaps** | Free for up to 5 GB of tiles (public) | `pmtiles upload` CLI or UI. | | **TileServer‑GL Cloud** | $10/mo for 10 GB | Same workflow as MapTiler. | | **OpenFreeMap** (public) | Free, but you must match their schema (OpenMapTiles). | Use their style URL directly; you can’t upload custom data. | These services give you a ready‑to‑use URL (`https://…/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`) and a TileJSON endpoint, so you can skip the `pmtiles` plugin entirely. --- ## 5. If you *must* stay with GeoJSON (e.g., live editing) Sometimes the data is constantly changing (user‑drawn parcels, real‑time updates). In that case you can still avoid the 180 MB monolith by: 1. **Chunking by tile** – split the dataset into a set of small GeoJSON files that correspond to a regular XYZ grid (e.g., 256 × 256 m tiles). 2. **Dynamic loading** – on `moveend` query the server for the tiles intersecting the current viewport (a simple REST endpoint that returns the appropriate GeoJSON chunk). 3. **Cache in the browser** – store fetched chunks in `IndexedDB` or a `Map` so you don’t re‑download them when panning back. This pattern mimics vector tiles but stays in pure GeoJSON. It’s more work on the backend and still incurs a lot of HTTP overhead, so it’s usually a stop‑gap while you move to true vector tiles. --- ## 6.
